1.e4 e5 2.Bc4.name: Bishop's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4.background: One of the oldest openings to be analysed, studied by Lucena and Ruy López and given its theoretical foundation by Philidor. It fell out of favour in the mid-nineteenth century after improvements for Black appeared. Bent Larsen was one of the few grandmasters to play it often, after first using it at the 1964 Interzonal, and Péter Lékó played it against Kramnik in the 2007 World Championship.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece with an attack on e4, so White must decide at once how to defend the pawn, and Black gets active play early. The usual quiet defence lets Black develop comfortably, but White can still play f2-f4 later, a delayed King's Gambit, so Black has to stay alert.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move but puts no pressure on e4, so White is free to choose the kind of game: a calm, familiar development, or a pawn sacrifice with f2-f4 in King's Gambit style, which Black must be ready for.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5.strategy: Mirrors White's bishop and develops it with an eye on f2, a symmetrical and solid set-up. White can steer the game into other openings or prepare d4 with c3, and Black must be ready for a pawn offered for quick play.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6.name: Bishop's Opening: Philidor Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6.background: Playable but rarely seen. Black seems to do better by delaying the idea one move, with 2...Nf6 3.d3 c6, the Paulsen Defence.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 to gain a tempo on the bishop and build a broad pawn centre. It costs time: the pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight and leaves e5 without support, so White can strike first in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 solidly, and after 3.Nf3 the game transposes to the Philidor Defence with White's bishop already on c4. The pawn limits the f8-bishop to e7 and cedes space, so Black is sound but passive.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Qe7.strategy: Covers e5 and f7 with the queen but shuts in the f8-bishop, which stays idle until the queen moves again or ...g6 follows. White develops freely and gains time by harassing the queen with a knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Ne7.strategy: Prepares ...d5, but the knight blocks the f8-bishop, and a knight on f6 serves the same aim from a better square. 3.Qh5 then hits e5 and threatens mate on f7, and only 3...Ng6 parries both.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Na6.strategy: Puts a knight on the rim, far from the centre, and does not defend e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once. 3.Bxa6 bxa6 would also wreck Black's queenside pawns.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early: it defends e5 and eyes f2 but takes f6 from the knight. 3.Nc3 followed by Nd5 attacks it with tempo, and White develops while Black spends moves on the queen.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Qg5.strategy: Attacks the undefended g2-pawn, but 3.Nf3 hits the queen and e5 at once. Taking with 3...Qxg2? fails to 4.Rg1 Qh3 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+, which wins the queen.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Qh4.strategy: Hits e4 and f2 at once, but 3.Qe2 defends e4 and prepares Nf3, which attacks the queen with tempo. After the queen retreats White has the lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bd6.strategy: Defends e5, but the bishop blocks the d-pawn, so ...d6 and ...d5 are impossible and the c8-bishop stays shut in. 3.Qh5 already threatens Qxf7#, and White develops freely against the clumsy set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bb4.strategy: Loses time: 3.c3 hits the bishop at once and prepares d4, so White builds the centre with tempo. On b4 the bishop bites only on the well-defended d2-pawn and does nothing for e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nh6.strategy: Covers f7 and eyes g4 and f5, but the rim knight does little in the centre. Once the d-pawn moves, Bxh6 gxh6 exchanges it for White's dark-squared bishop and doubles Black's kingside pawns.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop, but spends two wing moves on it while e5 and f7 are exposed to attack. The bishop simply retreats to b3.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops b4, but develops nothing and leaves e5 undefended. White uses the tempo to attack e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against the e4-pawn, but White holds e4 easily, and the slow move leaves f7 and e5 exposed to Qh5.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5.name: Bishop's Opening: Anderssen Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to draw the bishop off its diagonal, hoping for ...Bb7 against e4 and quick development. 3.Bxb5 simply takes it, and Black's compensation is too thin to justify the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c5.strategy: Leaves a permanent hole on d5 and develops nothing. The e5-pawn is left without support, and 3.Nf3 attacks it at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 d5.name: Bishop's Opening: Khan Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 d5.background: Analysis credits Black with fair compensation for the pawn, even if the gambit is objectively insufficient.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the bishop and the e4-pawn at once and offers the d-pawn for time. Black develops quickly after 3.exd5, but the gambit is objectively insufficient and White keeps the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f6.strategy: Defends e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and opens the a2-g8 diagonal to the c4-bishop, which then hinders castling short. 3.Qh5+ forces ...g6 or ...Ke7 and leaves lasting holes around the king.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5.name: Bishop's Opening: Calabrese Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5.background: Named after Greco's homeland, Calabria. It is considered dubious: the line recommended by Carl Jaenisch, 3.d3 Nf6 4.f4 d6 5.Nf3, gives White the advantage.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5.strategy: Hits e4 with the f-pawn and goes for a counterattack, but it weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the king's cover, so White keeps an edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto but develops nothing and loosens the dark squares around the king. 3.d4 strikes at e5 at once, and after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen already hits the rook on h8.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 g5.strategy: Grabs space on the kingside but develops nothing and gives up control of f6 and h6 for good. White hits e5 at once, and h2-h4 can later undermine the g5-pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's knight and bishop but develops nothing and leaves e5 without support. White uses the tempo to hit e5 at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 h5.strategy: Prevents Qh5 but weakens g5 and the kingside for no real gain. It develops nothing, and 3.Nf3 hits the undefended e5-pawn with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop. 3.Qh5 at once threatens Qxe5#, and the c4-bishop adds to the pressure on f7, so the king remains a target in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Be7.strategy: Aims for a compact, solid set-up but loses the e5-pawn to 3.Qh5, which hits e5 and threatens Qxf7# because the bishop takes away the king's escape square. After 3...Nc6? 4.Qxf7# ends the game at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: bxa3 or Nxa3 simply wins the piece, and Black gets nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5.strategy: Accepts the gambit pawn instead of retreating. White is a pawn up and can step the bishop back to safety when it is attacked, so Black has to show real compensation in open lines and a quick centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bb3.strategy: Withdraws along the same diagonal, keeping the bishop aimed at f7 and avoiding the gambit's complications. It declines a free pawn, though, so White has no extra material to play with and Black can go on gaining space on the queenside.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Be2.strategy: Retreats but keeps the b5-pawn under attack, so Black has to defend or push it. The bishop leaves its active diagonal toward f7, though, and the extra pawn is not yet won: sound, but clearly second-rate.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 c6.name: Bishop's Opening: Anderssen Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 c6.background: Adolf Anderssen played both this move and 3...f5 after 3.Bxb5.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 c6.strategy: Hits the bishop at once and prepares a broad pawn centre, the point of the gambit. The bishop retreats with the extra pawn still White's, so Black has to prove the compensation in open lines and quick development; White stays better, but this is the most direct way to fight for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 f5.name: Bishop's Opening: Thorold Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 f5.background: Adolf Anderssen played both this move and 3...c6 after 3.Bxb5.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 f5.strategy: The gambit's other main idea: rather than chase the bishop, Black hits e4 at once to open lines for the pieces. It loosens the king's diagonal and stays a pawn down, so White keeps the better game; after 4.d4, taking on e4 loses the rook on h8 to Qh5+ g6 Qxe5+.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 b5 3.Bxb5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a hit on the e4-pawn, so White has to look after the centre before cashing in the extra pawn. Black plays for quick development and an open centre as compensation, and keeps ...c6 in reserve to chase the bishop with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4.strategy: Attacks the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, and fights for the centre at once. With the pawn on c6 the natural knight defence of e5 is gone, so Black has to exchange or strike back in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e5 pawn, which nothing defends. The c6 pawn has taken the knight's natural square, so Black has to spend a move defending e5 and the plan of ...d5 arrives a tempo late.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and keeps the bishop on its diagonal. It is solid but passive: White gives up the central strike, so Black can break with ...d5 on its own terms and gets a full pawn centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5.strategy: The point of 2...c6: the pawn strikes at the centre, attacking the bishop and the e4 pawn while c6 and the queen defend it. Black opens the game with every piece still at home, which rewards whoever develops faster.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 exd4.strategy: Resolves the tension by capturing, leaving White free to regain the pawn with a developing move or to play for the initiative at once. Black keeps the c6 pawn ready for ...d5, but opens the e-file with its pieces still at home.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and keeps the structure compact, so Black can recapture in the centre as needed. It is passive: it gives up the central strike the c6 pawn was meant to prepare, and White keeps the freer game.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes first, so the pawn that attacked the bishop disappears and the e-file opens. The cost is the e-pawn, which until now held the centre together with d4, and Black recaptures with a gain of time on the bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.Bb3.strategy: Retreats to the diagonal where the bishop still eyes f7 and d5, but lets Black capture on e4. White has to win the pawn back with the centre open and the king's stay in the middle prolonged, a slightly worse version of the main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.Be2.strategy: Retreats out of the pawn's attack and keeps the bishop in the game, but gives up all pressure on f7 and leaves the bishop passive. Black takes the centre at once, and White can force a queen trade that keeps the material level, with no advantage left.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 cxd5.strategy: Restores the material and attacks the bishop again, while the c-pawn leaves the file for Black's rooks. The e5 pawn is still attacked by d4 and has no defender, so the bishop will be able to move with a threat.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 exd4.strategy: Captures on d4 first, so the pawn on d5 takes on c6 and the knight retakes: the material stays level. The d4 pawn is far advanced and becomes a target while White develops with tempo, so Black gains nothing over recapturing on d5.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Loses the queen for a bishop and a pawn: the bishop on c4 takes it at once, and ...cxd5 only recovers the bishop. Black has given up far too much material and has a lost position.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 c6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 cxd5 5.B.strategy: Saves the attacked bishop with check, so Black has to answer the check and the threat to take on e5 together. White gains time and trades the bishop for a piece that is not yet developed.

Retreats safely and keeps an eye on d5 and f7, but gives up the check that wins time. The e5 pawn is still attacked by d4, so Black has to defend it while developing, and White's bishop has lost its most active diagonal.

Keeps the bishop on a useful diagonal, but it blocks the d-pawn, and the pawn on e5 can advance with ...e4 and attack it again. White gains a flexible set-up at the price of time and a less harmonious pawn centre.

Blocks the check with the bishop and offers a trade. The b8-knight can recapture on d7 with a developing move that also defends e5, which is why Black can afford to leave that pawn alone for the moment.

Blocks the check with the knight, which is then pinned. White can give up the bishop for it, wrecking Black's pawn structure, and take on e5, a pawn Black cannot retake at once. Black has only the bishop pair to show for the pawn.
Blocks with the knight, which is pinned to the king: it cannot recapture on e5, so dxe5 wins a pawn. Black has no good way to win it back and the pinned knight is a continuing liability.
Trades White's light-squared bishop for Black's, ending the pressure the bishop has put on f7 since move two. The d4 pawn still attacks e5, so Black's recapture has to defend that pawn as well.

Develops and backs up the bishop on b5, so a trade is met by a recapture with the knight rather than by a lost piece. It also attacks the d5 pawn, which the bishop leaves without a defender. White keeps the d4 pressure on e5, but the game is level.

Defends the bishop on b5 and adds a second attacker on e5. If Black trades bishops, the queen recaptures with check. The queen is out early, though, and Black can answer by trading queens, which removes the pressure on e5.

The recapture that develops a piece and defends e5 in the same move. If White takes on e5, the knight recaptures on an active square, at the price of an isolated pawn on d5 that Black must look after.

Recaptures with the queen, but then nothing defends e5, and dxe5 wins a pawn that Black cannot regain at once. The queen on d7 also blocks the knight's route to defend. White keeps a lasting extra pawn.
Gives up castling and leaves the king in the open on d7. It also leaves the e5 pawn undefended, so dxe5 wins a pawn while the king stays exposed on the d-file.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5 3.d3.name: Bishop's Opening: Calabrese Countergambit, Jaenisch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5 3.d3.strategy: Defends the attacked e4 pawn with a pawn, so ...fxe4 can be met by dxe4, and opens the c1-bishop. It is a calm answer to a gambit that has loosened Black's own king, but it is slower than the sharper or the more developing replies.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5 3.f4.strategy: The sharp answer: the pawn hits e5 at once and fights for the centre while Black's own king is loosened. It is double-edged, though: White's king is loosened too, and the open e1-h4 diagonal allows ...Qh4+, so White has to play precisely.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a piece and develops at once, so ...fxe4 is met by Nxe4 with a lead in development. The safe route: White commits no pawn and keeps the bishop eyeing f7, while Black's king is exposed on the e8-h5 diagonal. It strikes less sharply at the centre than a pawn advance.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the f-pawn free, so White can strike with it later. The knight blocks the c-pawn, which rules out a broad pawn centre, and puts no pressure on e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: The most natural move: it develops a piece with an attack on e5, which the c6-knight defends, and heads for castling. White keeps the bishop on c4 aimed at f7 and enters a classical open game in which quick development and the fight for the centre decide.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.d3.strategy: Props up e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, keeping the knights flexible. White builds slowly and decides later between a quiet set-up and a strike with the f-pawn. It asks little of Black, who has time to develop comfortably.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Vienna Game: Stanley Variation, Three Knights Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: The most natural reply: it develops a piece with an attack on e4, which the knight on c3 guards. Black keeps a flexible, solid set-up and leaves White to choose between a quiet and a sharp game.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5.strategy: Mirrors White's bishop and aims at f2, but runs into the queen move to g4 at once: g7 loses its defender when the bishop leaves f8, and Black must give up castling or weaken the kingside to keep the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Be7.strategy: A modest development that keeps the bishop off the exposed c5 square, so the queen sortie to g4 is met by ...Bf6, which guards g7. The price is passivity: the bishop does nothing active, and White can take the initiative in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qg4.strategy: Attacks g7 at once: the pawn has no defender now that the bishop has left f8, and the rook on h8 stands behind it. Black must defend with a concession, and the natural-looking queen move runs into a trap.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and attacks e5, which the c6-knight defends. White gives up the sharp queen sortie for a harmonious set-up, with the king ready to castle at once: a classical, low-risk game in which both sides develop freely.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.d3.strategy: Supports e4 and opens the c1-bishop, a slow build-up that keeps both the queen sortie and an f-pawn advance in reserve. It also gives Black time to develop with an attack on e4, so White's best chance of an edge is not used.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qg4 Qf6.strategy: Walks into the trap: the queen defends g7 and doubles on f2, but 5.Nd5 attacks it and the c7 pawn at once. After 5...Qxf2+ 6.Kd1 the white king is safe enough while g7 and c7 hang, and Nxc7+ would fork king and rook.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qg4 Kf8.strategy: Guards g7 with the king itself and keeps the pawn structure intact. Black gives up castling, but White's queen has no target and the pieces can be developed without concessions. An awkward-looking but sound answer that avoids the traps.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qg4 g6.strategy: Shuts the queen out of g7 by advancing the pawn, which f7 and h7 guard. Black keeps castling but weakens the dark squares around the king, since the bishop has left f8, and White's bishop keeps up the pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qg4 Qf6 5..name: Vienna Game: Stanley Variation, Meitner-Mieses Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qg4 Qf6 5..strategy: Springs the trap with a double attack on the queen and c7, while the queen on g4 still hits g7. Black can take f2 with check, but the king steps to d1 and White's threats against g7 and c7 outweigh the lost pawn.
Offers a queen trade that removes the pressure on f2 and defuses the position. White stays level and sound, but throws away the initiative and the attack on g7, so Black has nothing to fear.
Grabs the pawn and loses the queen: the queen on f6 guards g7, so ...Qxg7 takes White's queen for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3.name: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3.background: The name reflects its mixed parentage: the position can be reached from the Bishop's Opening and, by several move orders, from the Vienna Game.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Backs up e4 with a pawn, which frees the c3-knight from guard duty and opens the c1-bishop. White builds up slowly, keeping the bishop on c4 pointed at f7 and the choice of plan open.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for a quick attack: the f-pawn bears on e5, the f-file opens and the bishop already eyes f7. It is a real gambit with real risk: White is a pawn down if the attack fizzles, and the e1-h4 diagonal is open.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and attacks e5, which the c6-knight defends, at the price of blocking the f-pawn. White steers into a classical development in which both sides castle and play for the centre. It is solid and low-risk, but gives up the quick f-pawn strike.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to the active diagonal towards f2, White's weakest point, and keeps the pawn structure intact. Black stays flexible and ready to castle, and leaves White to decide how sharp the game becomes.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the c3-knight to the king, since d2 is empty, and threatens ...Bxc3+ to double White's pawns. Black uses the pin to put pressure on e4 and White's centre and decides when to give up the bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Na5.strategy: Hits the bishop so that White must give it up or retreat. The exchange costs White the bishop that eyes f7 and usually saddles White with doubled pawns, while Black keeps both bishops; the price is a few tempi spent on a knight move.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.strategy: A modest developing move that prepares castling and keeps the pawn structure intact. It avoids the active diagonals, so it asks White little: the game stays level, but Black has to let White decide how the centre develops.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bb4 5.N.name: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Hromádka Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Guards c3 a second time, so ...Bxc3+ can be met by a knight recapture and White's pawns stay intact, with the bishop pair as a bonus. The pin remains, but it now costs White little, and the knight also helps a later f-pawn advance.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bb4 5.B.strategy: Breaks the pin by developing the c1-bishop, so ...Bxc3 is met by a bishop recapture that keeps the pawns intact and leaves White with both bishops. A natural, solid answer that asks Black what the bishop on b4 is for.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and eyes e5, but leaves the pin in place. After ...Bxc3+ White recaptures with the b-pawn, getting the bishop pair and a half-open b-file at the price of doubled, weak pawns on the c-file.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5 5.f.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once, the point of developing the c3-knight first: the f-pawn is free to advance and open the f-file. The price is a looser king, since with f2 empty Black's bishop bears directly on the knight on g1.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight and attacks e5, which the c6-knight defends, steering into a classical set-up with castling close. It blocks the f-pawn, though, giving up the quick strike the c3-knight prepared.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5 5.B.strategy: Pins the f6-knight against the queen to unsettle Black's centre. The pin is mild: Black can challenge it with ...h6, and the bishop has spent a tempo for little. Playable, but it does not test Black.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5 5.f.strategy: Holds e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Black chooses a solid set-up over an immediate counterstrike and keeps the bishop on c5 pointing at g1, while the f4 pawn is not yet allowed to open the centre.

Trades Black's e-pawn for White's f-pawn: the c1-bishop regains the pawn at once. White is left with the only central pawn on e4 and free development, so Black removes the tension but gives up a share of the centre.

Castles at once and leaves the tension in the centre as it is. White can resolve it by capturing on e5, and the position opens with Black's king already tucked away; sound but passive, since e5 gets no extra defender.

Brings the kingside knight into play and adds a second attacker to e5, which d6 and the c6-knight defend. It also prepares castling, but the knight now stands in front of the queen, a weakness Black can use.
Takes on e5 straight away and opens the f-file, but releases the pressure the f-pawn put on e5. After the recapture the centre is level again and White's gain of space is gone. Playable but harmless.

Goes after the bishop on c5, which eyes the weakened g1 square, hoping to trade it off. The knight leaves the centre, e4 is now held by the d-pawn alone, and Black can retreat the bishop and leave the knight offside. Playable but slow.
Pins the knight against the queen, so any move of the knight exposes the queen, and threatens ...Bxf3 to remove an attacker of e5. Black develops with a purpose and adds pressure on the centre.

Castles at once, getting the king to safety before White opens the f-file. Black keeps a solid position with the bishop on c5 still aimed at g1 and waits to see what White does with the centre; less pointed than the pin.
Takes the pawn, but the c1-bishop regains it at once and now eyes the diagonal towards d6. Black's central pawn is traded for White's f-pawn, which leaves White the only pawn in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f4 Nxe4.strategy: Accepts the pawn with the knight, which is protected by a tactic: 5.Nxe4 d5 attacks bishop and knight at once. White gets open lines against e5 and a lead in development, so Black must hold the extra pawn carefully.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f4 exf4.strategy: Wins a pawn for the moment, but the f4 pawn is hard to hold, and White gets open lines and quick development for it. The e5 pawn disappears, and White can strike in the centre with tempo. A greedy but playable choice.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f4 d6.strategy: Holds e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, a solid set-up that ignores the gambit. White can still open the f-file by capturing on e5, with the bishop on c4 already aimed at f7, so Black has to stay alert.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f4 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Stanley Variation, Bronstein Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f4 Nxe4 5..strategy: Declines to trade on e4, where ...d5 would fork bishop and knight, and develops with a second attack on e5 beside the f-pawn.
